newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe welcomes global deal on telecoms trade.
newsitem.headline: Europe welcomes global deal on telecoms trade.

text.p: European Union nations on Monday welcomed the global telecoms trade deal hammered out at the weekend and many predicted it would give rise to employment growth and investment opportunities for years to come.
"This is a deal of truly immense proportions," said Peter Guilford, spokesman for the European Union's Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.
"This is a pretty powerful cocktail for economic growth -- not just for telecoms but for world trade as a whole," he added.
In Geneva on Saturday, some 68 countries agreed to a package of liberalisation measures which will come into effect next year -- although some countries won concessions to delay for a year or two.

Services chiefly affected will be voice operated telephone systems and networks, domestic and international data transmission, global fax communications, private telephone circuits and mobile systems.

The only "blemish" in the deal, according to the European Commission, was Washington's hint that the U.S. would not abide by commitments regarding so-called "direct-to-home" services, including video-on-demand via telephone lines.
Guilford said, however, that if the issue was raised in the future, the EU would "vigorously challenge Washington at an appropriate forum".
In London British Telecommunications Plc said it was delighted by the pact which opens up most of the world's $600 billion telecoms market.
"We are still studying the details but we believe that the outcome offers almost every citizen in the world the opportunity to experience the benefits of competition," a spokeswoman said.
British Science and Technology Minister Ian Taylor predicted a "boom" for world telecoms.
Taylor said some analysts were predicting a further $1 trillion in additional growth over the next 10-15 years, 20 billion pounds ($32 billion) worth of which could be for the UK alone.
In Bonn, the German government said its 1996 partial liberalisation of domestic market helped forge the deal.
"We implemented one of the world's most liberal telecommunications laws last year and with our law we helped to drive this process," a spokesman for Post and Telecommunications Ministry said.
Deutsche Telekom AG, Germany's dominant telecoms player that enjoys a monopoly on basic phone services until 1998, welcomed the deal and said it would enhance global competition.

Most countries in the EU will drop the last barriers to full competition in telecommunications on January 1, 1998. Some segments of the industry are already open to competition, such as data services, mobile communications and cable television.
Ireland's Telecom Eireann said the accord would lead to significant reductions in Irish telephone rates.
"Competition in telecoms will continue to force prices downward," Gerry O'Sullivan, head of corporate communications at Telecom Eireann, told Reuters.
Irish long distance telephone rates were likely to be cut by 50 percent over the next three years, he said.
Spain, considered by analysts to be one of the EU's more closed markets, was still studying the implications of the deal -- brokered on all 15 EU members states' behalf by the Commission.

"Spain has already agreed to open its telecommunications market from 1998, so this EU deal has little impact. It's an agreement in very general terms and doesn't really add much to what is already going on," said a telecoms analyst who requested anonymity.

In Portugal, Jose Freire, telecommunications analyst of Espirito Santo Research in Lisbon told Reuters that dominant telecommunications operator Portugal Telecom, which charges among the highest rates for international calls in Europe, would not feel much impact from the WTO pact as the liberalisation of the Portuguese telecommunications market had been delayed until 2000, two years after most other EU states must act.
"What you'll see is a sharp drop in international tariffs by European operators," Freire said. "Portugal Telecom will be less affected than some others because its market is protected until 2000."
